Yet, examining their actual achievements, Master Han’s Inquiry into the Way (Yuan dao) elucidated the meaning of the Way and virtue and vigorously rejected errors that had the appearance of truth. This was assuredly beyond Master Liu’s capacity to match. Moreover, Master Liu failed to guard against association with unworthy men and ultimately brought upon himself the sorrow of banishment to a distant place. Did he not thereby further estrange himself from the Way of the sages?

When the fashion for cramped and awkward expression [?] became rampant, Song prose became corrupted. Ouyang Xiu arose to transform it, honoring refinement and rejecting superficiality: he was what one calls the Han Yu of the Song. The Su brothers followed and responded to him. With their marvelous command of rhetorical expansion, contraction, and variation, they were indeed extraordinary talents in the realm. Thus those who discuss Song prose…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
必美乎歐蘇焉然考其時則周子之太極
圖張子之西銘程子之易傳春秋傳序究
極天人之蘊發明聖經之旨亦非歐蘇之
所能及也况歐之性非所先蘇之以術談
經又自外於聖人之道乎故論唐之文至
韓愈正矣然其時又不有陸宣公乎行在
諸疏經國弘猷奉天一詔聞者感泣茲固
其文也然其上不負天子下不負所學無
愧平生之言寧人負我無我負人深合聖
===
經之旨則又不特論諫之可法而已所謂
智如子房而學則過才如賈誼而術不疎
蘇子真知言哉論宋之文至周程張子偉
矣然其時又不有朱子乎傳註之作折衷
羣籍告君之言不離誠正茲固其文也然
其居敬以立其體窮理以致其知克己以
滅其私存誠以踐其實則亦不特著述之
可傳而已所謂傳濂洛之正統集諸儒之
大成吳澄氏豈溢美哉之二公者皆庶幾
punctuated:
必美乎歐蘇焉。然考其時，則周子之《太極圖》、張子之《西銘》、程子之《易傳》《春秋傳序》，究極天人之蘊，發明聖經之旨，亦非歐蘇之所能及也。况歐之「性非所先」，蘇之以術談經，又自外於聖人之道乎？故論唐之文，至韓愈正矣。然其時又不有陸宣公乎？行在諸疏，經國弘猷；奉天一詔，聞者感泣：茲固其文也。然其上不負天子，下不負所學，無愧平生之言，「寧人負我，無我負人」，深合聖經之旨，則又不特論諫之可法而已。所謂「智如子房而學則過，才如賈誼而術不疎」，蘇子真知言哉！

論宋之文，至周程張子偉矣。然其時又不有朱子乎？傳註之作，折衷羣籍；告君之言，不離誠正：茲固其文也。然其居敬以立其體，窮理以致其知，克己以滅其私，存誠以踐其實，則亦不特著述之可傳而已。所謂「傳濂洛之正統，集諸儒之大成」，吳澄氏豈溢美哉？之二公者，皆庶幾
translation_en:
…will invariably praise Ouyang Xiu and Su Shi. Yet if we examine their age, Master Zhou’s Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, Master Zhang’s Western Inscription, and Master Cheng’s Commentary on the Changes and Preface to the Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals explored the deepest mysteries of Heaven and humanity and elucidated the purport of the sages’ classics. These, too, were beyond the reach of Ouyang and Su. Moreover, with Ouyang’s assertion that “human nature is not the first priority” and Su’s discussion of the classics in terms of expedient techniques, did they not place themselves outside the Way of the sages? Thus, in discussing Tang prose, we reach true correctness with Han Yu. Yet was there not also Lu Xuangong in his day? His memorials submitted to the emperor’s temporary residence offered grand plans for governing the realm; his single edict issued at Fengtian moved those who heard it to tears. These were certainly achievements of his writing. Yet he neither failed the Son of Heaven above nor betrayed his own learning below, and he lived without dishonoring his lifelong declaration: “Better that others betray me than that I betray others.” This accorded profoundly with the purport of the sages’ classics. Thus, it was not merely his arguments and remonstrances that deserved to serve as models. As was said of him, “His wisdom equaled Zifang’s, but his learning surpassed it; his talent equaled Jia Yi’s, but his methods were free of shortcomings.” Master Su truly spoke with discernment!

In discussing Song prose, we reach greatness with Masters Zhou, Cheng, and Zhang. Yet was there not also Master Zhu in their day? His commentaries and annotations weighed and reconciled the many books; his counsel to the ruler never departed from sincerity of intention and rectification of the mind. These were certainly achievements of his writing. Yet he maintained reverent attentiveness to establish his moral foundation, investigated principles to extend his knowledge, mastered himself to eliminate selfishness, and preserved sincerity to put these truths into practice. Thus, it was not merely his writings that deserved transmission. As was said of him, “He transmitted the orthodox succession of Lian and Luo and brought the achievements of the Confucian scholars to their fullest culmination.” Was Wu Cheng’s praise excessive? These two gentlemen both came close to…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
乎聖賢之文者也然合而論之諫行言聽
經國制變則朱子不如宣公之大立德立
言傳道教人則宣公不如朱子之久要之
朱子載道之文上承道統之正宣公不得
而與也善乎其徒黃幹之言曰孔子沒曾
子子思繼其微至孟子而始著孟子沒周
程張子繼其絕至朱子而始明玆言也其
斯文之斷案矣乎噫六經孔孟之文不可
得而續矣論文者取衷於朱子斯可矣聖
===
人自然之文不可得而見矣爲文者取法
於朱子亦足矣雖然文不可以易爲也而
所以昌之者存乎氣道不可以襲取也而
所以明之者存乎心蓋心者道之管也氣
者文之充也故爲文者莫先乎治心其次
莫若養氣心以爲主氣以出之然後可以
不離於道而昌其辭學者執是道以往則
載道之文其庶幾乎周子所謂篤實而藝
書美愛而久傳者或在玆也不然亦虛車
punctuated:
乎聖賢之文者也。然合而論之，諫行言聽，經國制變，則朱子不如宣公之大；立德立言，傳道教人，則宣公不如朱子之久。要之，朱子載道之文，上承道統之正，宣公不得而與也。善乎其徒黃幹之言曰：「孔子沒，曾子、子思繼其微，至孟子而始著；孟子沒，周、程、張子繼其絕，至朱子而始明。」玆言也，其斯文之斷案矣乎！噫！六經孔孟之文，不可得而續矣，論文者取衷於朱子，斯可矣。聖人自然之文，不可得而見矣，爲文者取法於朱子，亦足矣。

雖然，文不可以易爲也，而所以昌之者存乎氣；道不可以襲取也，而所以明之者存乎心。蓋心者，道之管也；氣者，文之充也。故爲文者莫先乎治心，其次莫若養氣。心以爲主，氣以出之，然後可以不離於道而昌其辭。學者執是道以往，則載道之文，其庶幾乎！周子所謂篤實而藝，書美愛而久傳者，或在玆也。不然，亦虛車
translation_en:
…approached the writings of the sages and worthies. Yet, considering the two together, in having remonstrances acted upon and counsel heeded, governing the state and managing unforeseen changes, Master Zhu fell short of Duke Xuan’s greatness; in establishing virtue and enduring teachings, transmitting the Way and instructing others, Duke Xuan fell short of Master Zhu’s lasting influence. In essence, Master Zhu’s writings, which bore the Way, inherited from above the orthodox transmission of the Way: here Duke Xuan could not match him. How well his disciple Huang Gan put it: “After Confucius died, Zengzi and Zisi carried on his teachings when they had become obscure; only with Mencius did they become manifest. After Mencius died, Masters Zhou, Cheng, and Zhang renewed the severed transmission; only with Master Zhu did it become clear.” Surely these words constitute the definitive judgment on this cultural tradition! Alas! The writings of the Six Classics, Confucius, and Mencius cannot be continued. Those who judge writing may rightly take Master Zhu as their standard. The sages’ naturally accomplished writing can no longer be witnessed; for those who compose, it is sufficient to take Master Zhu as their model.

Nevertheless, writing cannot be undertaken lightly: what makes it flourish lies in vital energy, or qi. The Way cannot be acquired by imitation: what makes it clear lies in the mind. The mind is the conduit of the Way, and vital energy gives writing its fullness. Thus, for those who write, nothing takes precedence over ordering the mind; next, nothing is better than nourishing vital energy. Let the mind govern and vital energy give expression to it: only then can one make one’s language flourish without departing from the Way. If students proceed by holding to this method, they may come close to producing writing that bears the Way. What Master Zhou described as being grounded in sincerity and endowed with artistry, beautifully written, cherished, and transmitted for generations [?], may lie here. Otherwise, it is merely an empty carriage…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
耳執事何庸焉
第三問
石磐
同考試官教諭祝批議論有據詞致亦工進
士也
考試官學正李批敷敘有體斷制不差
程式之文也
考試官教授向批詳贍
達經制之宜者而後知聖人制治之法通
===
損益之故者而後知聖人制法之詳夫聖
人立法以維治非聖人意也勢也世非忘
言則法不得以不立日入于多事則制不
容以不詳故創法以制治存之爲百王之
典因典以貽則垂之爲萬世之經此皆聖
人精神心術之運裁成輔相之能也議法
者不達其宜疑之所以生也猶輪人之巧
不足而欲廢大匠之規矩者也用法者弗
獲其效沮之所以生也猶醫人不求標本
punctuated:
耳，執事何庸焉？

第三問
石磐

同考試官教諭祝批：「議論有據，詞致亦工，進士也。」
考試官學正李批：「敷敘有體，斷制不差，程式之文也。」
考試官教授向批：「詳贍。」

達經制之宜者，而後知聖人制治之法；通損益之故者，而後知聖人制法之詳。夫聖人立法以維治，非聖人意也，勢也。世非忘言，則法不得以不立；日入于多事，則制不容以不詳。故創法以制治，存之爲百王之典；因典以貽則，垂之爲萬世之經。此皆聖人精神心術之運，裁成輔相之能也。議法者不達其宜，疑之所以生也，猶輪人之巧不足而欲廢大匠之規矩者也。用法者弗獲其效，沮之所以生也，猶醫人不求標本
translation_en:
…that is all. What use would you, sir, have for it?

Third Policy Question
Shi Pan 石磐

Associate Examiner Zhu, Instructor, comments: “His arguments have sound foundations, and his expression is accomplished. He is fit to be a metropolitan graduate (jinshi).”
Examiner Li, Instructor, comments: “The exposition is properly structured, and the judgments are sound. This essay provides a model to follow.”
Examiner Xiang, Instructor, comments: “Detailed and ample.”

Only those who understand the appropriateness of established institutions can understand the sages’ methods of ordering government; only those who comprehend the reasons for removing and adding provisions can understand the detail of the sages’ legislation. The sages established laws to sustain good government not out of personal inclination, but because circumstances required it. Since the world was not one in which words could be forgotten [?], laws had to be established; as affairs grew more numerous by the day, institutions necessarily became more detailed. Thus they created laws to order government and preserved them as statutes for the succession of kings; drawing upon these statutes, they bequeathed standards, handing them down as enduring norms for all ages. All this manifested the workings of the sages’ spiritual energies and arts of the mind, and their capacity to shape things to completion and assist their proper development.

Those who discuss laws without understanding their appropriateness thereby give rise to doubts. They are like a wheelwright whose skill is inadequate, yet who wishes to discard the master craftsman’s compass and square. Those who apply laws without obtaining their intended results thereby become discouraged. They are like a physician who fails to investigate the symptoms and root causes…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
之理而歸咎于古人之方者也周禮之不
幸類是其不明不行也宜哉執事以周禮
策諸生而致疑於建官出令之詳此愚生
之所以不容不辯也夫周公相成王以成
一代之治斟酌損益著爲定制周禮者所
以紀其經緯彌綸之迹也其規模統體之
極其大條理節目之盡其詳具有成書固
無俟於贅矣顧流言肆而東居之轍遠嬴
計左而瓜丘之焰張其志弗竟而法之弗
===
行是以弗著弗察無惑乎後人是非疑信
之不一雖經程朱胡蘇之辯論而終莫取
衷豈聖人之制可疑哉無亦議之者之見
爾自今觀之政莫重於建官而法必先於
出令建官惟其人出令惟其時治之所係
不小也是故政不可以一人理任職親民
以計治弊訟官之不可已也然祿以馭富
官眾而祿將奚從出乎唐虞惟百夏商官
倍亦克用乂周禮五官之屬眾至數萬執
punctuated: 之理，而歸咎于古人之方者也。《周禮》之不幸類是，其不明不行也，宜哉！執事以《周禮》策諸生，而致疑於建官出令之詳，此愚生之所以不容不辯也。夫周公相成王，以成一代之治，斟酌損益，著爲定制。《周禮》者，所以紀其經緯彌綸之迹也。其規模統體之極其大，條理節目之盡其詳，具有成書，固無俟於贅矣。顧流言肆而東居之轍遠，嬴計左而瓜丘之焰張，其志弗竟而法之弗行，是以弗著弗察，無惑乎後人是非疑信之不一。雖經程朱胡蘇之辯論，而終莫取衷，豈聖人之制可疑哉？無亦議之者之見爾。自今觀之，政莫重於建官，而法必先於出令。建官惟其人，出令惟其時，治之所係不小也。是故政不可以一人理，任職親民，以計治弊訟，官之不可已也。然祿以馭富，官眾而祿將奚從出乎？唐虞惟百，夏商官倍，亦克用乂。《周禮》五官之屬，眾至數萬，執
translation_en:
…the principles involved, but instead lay the blame on the prescriptions of the ancients. The misfortune suffered by the Rites of Zhou is of this kind. Little wonder that it has neither been understood nor put into practice! You, honored Examiner, have set the Rites of Zhou as a policy question for us candidates, expressing doubts about its detailed provisions for establishing offices and issuing commands. This is why I, an unworthy student, cannot refrain from offering a defense.

The Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng in bringing the government of an entire age to fruition. Weighing what should be removed or added, he set down fixed institutions. The Rites of Zhou records the traces of his work in ordering and comprehensively organizing government. Its framework and overall structure are vast in the utmost degree; its arrangements and specific provisions are detailed to the fullest extent. All are contained in the completed book, and further elaboration is surely unnecessary. Yet slander ran rampant, and his journey to reside in the east took him far away; the schemes of Ying went awry, and the flames at Guaqiu blazed up [?]. His aspirations remained unfulfilled, and his institutions were not implemented. Thus they were neither made manifest nor clearly examined. It is no wonder that later generations have differed in their judgments of right and wrong, doubt and belief. Although Cheng, Zhu, Hu, and Su have debated the matter, no settled judgment has ultimately been reached. Can the sage’s institutions really be doubtful? Is it not merely a matter of the views of those who discuss them?

Viewed from the present, nothing in government is more important than establishing offices, and rules must precede the issuing of commands. Establishing offices depends on finding the right people; issuing commands depends on choosing the right time. Their bearing on good government is no small matter. Government therefore cannot be managed by one person alone. Officials must undertake duties and attend to the people, assess administration, and adjudicate lawsuits: offices cannot be dispensed with. Yet stipends are the means of regulating wealth. If officials are numerous, where will their stipends come from? Under Tang and Yu there were only a hundred offices; under Xia and Shang their number doubled, yet these dynasties were still able to achieve orderly government. In the Rites of Zhou, the personnel subordinate to the five principal offices number in the tens of thousands. You…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
事疑其官之衆而欲究其祿之所自出誠
有見也然内外之備官者制之詳也官事
之必攝者制之善也故周公以冢宰兼三
公召公以三公兼司徒師旅之將帥卽王
朝之卿士皆因事設官事已而官廢則雖
衆而不爲冗矣乃若田以井授公私内外
之有其差祿以田賦卿士大夫之有所仰
此井田世祿相須而行何有於祿之不給
耶不然使之自食其力祿不足好于其家
===
===
室人徧謫豈先王恤人之私哉令不可以
弗豫申命行事以鼓舞萬民令之不可已
也然命之靡常視聽惑而民將奚以從乎
古者爲而不有應而不求周禮歲朔孟仲
凡大聚會月必屢至執事疑其令之煩而
慮其爲民之擾固其宜也然會以作事者
義之盡也而徵以時會者仁之至也故飲
射之法以州長行之讀法之法以黨正行
之象魏之布夾日而斂則令之素定民之
punctuated:
事疑其官之衆，而欲究其祿之所自出，誠有見也。然内外之備官者，制之詳也；官事之必攝者，制之善也。故周公以冢宰兼三公，召公以三公兼司徒；師旅之將帥，卽王朝之卿士。皆因事設官，事已而官廢，則雖衆而不爲冗矣。乃若田以井授，公私内外之有其差；祿以田賦，卿士大夫之有所仰。此井田世祿相須而行，何有於祿之不給耶？不然，使之自食其力，祿不足好于其家，室人徧謫，豈先王恤人之私哉？
令不可以弗豫，申命行事，以鼓舞萬民，令之不可已也。然命之靡常，視聽惑，而民將奚以從乎？古者爲而不有，應而不求。《周禮》歲朔孟仲，凡大聚會，月必屢至。執事疑其令之煩，而慮其爲民之擾，固其宜也。然會以作事者，義之盡也；而徵以時會者，仁之至也。故飲射之法，以州長行之；讀法之法，以黨正行之；象魏之布，夾日而斂。則令之素定，民之
translation_en:
…you question the multitude of officials and wish to investigate where their stipends came from: this is indeed perceptive. Yet the provision of a full complement of officials within and outside the capital shows the comprehensiveness of the institutional design; the requirement that official duties be performed concurrently shows its excellence. Thus the Duke of Zhou, as Grand Steward, concurrently held office as one of the Three Dukes, while the Duke of Shao, as one of the Three Dukes, concurrently served as Minister of Education. Commanders of armies and brigades were themselves ministers of the royal court. Offices were established in response to tasks and abolished when those tasks were finished. Thus, although numerous, they were not superfluous. As for land, it was allotted according to the well-field system, with distinctions between public and private holdings and between inner and outer areas. Stipends were provided through levies on the land, giving ministers and grand masters a source of support. The well-field system and hereditary stipends thus operated in mutual dependence. How could stipends have been insufficient? Otherwise, if officials were made to support themselves by their own labor, with stipends insufficient to secure their families’ goodwill and everyone in their households reproaching them, would this accord with the former kings’ concern for people’s private needs?
Orders must be prepared in advance. Commands are reiterated and affairs carried out to inspire the myriad people: orders cannot be dispensed with. Yet if commands constantly change, confusing what people see and hear, how will they know what to follow? The ancients acted without claiming possession and responded without seeking anything. In the Rites of Zhou, at the beginning of the year and the month, and in the first and second months of the seasons, the various great assemblies necessarily occurred repeatedly each month. It is certainly reasonable that you should question the frequency of these orders and fear that they disturbed the people. Yet assembling people to carry out affairs fulfills righteousness, while summoning them to assemble at appropriate times represents the utmost benevolence. Thus the procedures for drinking and archery ceremonies were administered by the District Chief, and those for reading out the laws by the Neighborhood Head. Laws displayed on the palace gate towers were taken down after ten days. Thus the orders were settled in advance, and the people’s…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
素孚雖煩而不為擾矣矧其振旅詢事而
隨地以致民蒐彌田狩而因時以舉事供
給徵召以有常守而何至於民之不堪邪
不然驅耕夫而役之不得盡力於農畝舍
我穡事豈先王重民之務哉於以見周公
之立法也隨事建官不豫官以待事因時
致令不煩令以勞民此良法美意周道之
所以長也然官非其人民受其殃好煩其
令雖令不從此則聖人所大懼也故曰官
===
不必備惟其人又曰愼乃出令令出惟行
此又其法外意也知此則選用雖衆固不
病於倖進之私徵會雖煩自不患於非時
之擾矣奈之何去聖愈遠而疑之愈衆或
以王制不合於是有成周理財之疑班爵
不合於是有六國陰謀之疑蓋至於十論
七難之作而其言益肆矣一用於劉歆益重乎新室
補於宇文之治再用於蘇綽無
之誣蓋至於青苗手實之行而其法益病
punctuated: 素孚，雖煩而不為擾矣。矧其振旅詢事，而隨地以致民；蒐彌田狩，而因時以舉事。供給徵召，以有常守，而何至於民之不堪邪？不然，驅耕夫而役之，不得盡力於農畝，舍我穡事，豈先王重民之務哉？於以見周公之立法也，隨事建官，不豫官以待事；因時致令，不煩令以勞民。此良法美意，周道之所以長也。然官非其人，民受其殃；好煩其令，雖令不從。此則聖人所大懼也。故曰：「官不必備，惟其人。」又曰：「愼乃出令，令出惟行。」此又其法外意也。知此，則選用雖衆，固不病於倖進之私；徵會雖煩，自不患於非時之擾矣。奈之何去聖愈遠，而疑之愈衆？或以王制不合，於是有成周理財之疑；班爵不合，於是有六國陰謀之疑。蓋至於十論七難之作，而其言益肆矣。一用於劉歆，益重乎新室，補於宇文之治，再用於蘇綽，無之誣。蓋至於青苗手實之行，而其法益病
translation_en: …long trusted by the people, so that even frequent commands cause no disturbance. Moreover, troops were mustered and affairs examined, and the people summoned according to locality; the seasonal hunts [?] were conducted, and undertakings initiated according to the season. Supplies and requisitions followed established rules: how could they become unbearable to the people? Otherwise, to drive farmers into service, preventing them from devoting their full strength to their fields and making them abandon their agricultural work—could this be the former kings’ commitment to the people’s livelihood? From this we see how the Duke of Zhou established institutions: he created offices as affairs required, rather than appointing officials beforehand to await affairs; he issued commands as the season required, rather than burdening the people with excessive commands. These sound institutions and benevolent intentions explain why the Way of Zhou endured. Yet when offices are held by unsuitable men, the people suffer; when rulers delight in multiplying commands, even their commands go unheeded. This was what the sages greatly feared. Thus it is said: “Offices need not all be filled; what matters is finding the right men.” It is also said: “Be cautious in issuing commands; once issued, commands must be carried out.” Here, too, lies the intention beyond the institutions themselves. Understanding this, one sees that even numerous appointments need not suffer from favoritism toward those seeking advancement through undeserved good fortune; even frequent summons and assemblies need not cause the disturbance of demands made at improper times. Why, then, have doubts multiplied as we grow ever more distant from the sages? Some, finding discrepancies with the Royal Regulations, came to suspect the account of financial administration in the Zhou dynasty; finding discrepancies in the ranking of noble titles, they came to suspect a clandestine scheme of the Six States. By the time the Ten Discourses and Seven Objections were written, such assertions had become still more unrestrained. It was first employed by Liu Xin, “increasing the weight upon the Xin dynasty”; “assistance to the rule of Yuwen”; employed a second time by Su Chuo; “without … the accusation” [?—the transcribed clauses here appear out of order]. By the time the Green Sprouts loans and the declarations of household assets were put into practice, these institutions were subjected to still greater criticism…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
矣不知五等通於天下難施於侯國孟子
言於去籍無以考其詳其矛盾相反宜世
議之紛紛也或欲行於上而難其任或欲
究其用而非其時其枘鑿不入宜致用之
弗效也然則周禮非真可疑弗求其實則
通變不知周禮非不可用任匪其人則扞
格無成嘗試考之其建官之制固在也失
之者將必有為人擇官苟取充位其始也
冗雜同途其既也根據莫解積薪之喻所
===
以有漢人之嘆也出令之法固在也失之
者將必有簿書期會責所不堪其始也若
憂之太殷其究也則擾之已甚種樹之術
是以啓唐人之論也然則議周禮者失周
禮者爾豈周禮之可議哉雖然古今者時
也經制者法也變通者人也時不相沿而
法因以異故周之建官後世多襲其迹而
召會徵令以施之今則擾矣故曰化而裁
之存乎變神而明之存乎人
punctuated:
矣。不知五等通於天下，難施於侯國；孟子言於去籍，無以考其詳。其矛盾相反，宜世議之紛紛也。或欲行於上而難其任，或欲究其用而非其時，其枘鑿不入，宜致用之弗效也。然則《周禮》非真可疑，弗求其實，則通變不知；《周禮》非不可用，任匪其人，則扞格無成。嘗試考之，其建官之制固在也，失之者將必有為人擇官，苟取充位。其始也，冗雜同途；其既也，根據莫解。積薪之喻，所以有漢人之嘆也。出令之法固在也，失之者將必有簿書期會，責所不堪。其始也，若憂之太殷；其究也，則擾之已甚。種樹之術，是以啓唐人之論也。然則議《周禮》者，失《周禮》者爾，豈《周禮》之可議哉！

雖然，古今者，時也；經制者，法也；變通者，人也。時不相沿，而法因以異。故周之建官，後世多襲其迹，而召會徵令，以施之今，則擾矣。故曰：「化而裁之存乎變，神而明之存乎人。」
translation_en:
…indeed. They fail to understand that the five ranks of nobility applied throughout the realm but were difficult to implement within the domains of the feudal lords. Mencius spoke of the removal of the records, leaving no means of examining the details. Given these contradictions and discrepancies, it is understandable that subsequent opinions have been so divided. Some wished to implement these institutions from above but found the task difficult; others wished to realize their full usefulness, but the time was unsuitable. Like tenons that do not fit their mortises, they naturally failed to produce results in practice. Thus the Rites of Zhou is not truly grounds for doubt: without seeking its substance, one cannot understand how to adapt to change. Nor is the Rites of Zhou unusable: if those entrusted with its implementation are unsuitable, obstruction and failure follow.

Let us examine this. Its system for establishing offices certainly remains available, but those who misconstrue it will inevitably choose offices to suit particular people, merely seeking to fill the posts. At first, superfluous and miscellaneous appointees advance along the same path; eventually, they become so firmly entrenched that they cannot be dislodged. This is what prompted the Han man's lament in his analogy of piling up firewood. Its methods for issuing commands certainly remain available, but those who misconstrue them will inevitably impose paperwork and deadlines, demanding what people cannot bear. At first, they seem excessively solicitous for the people; in the end, they harass them beyond measure. This is what prompted the Tang man's discussion of the art of planting trees. Thus those who criticize the Rites of Zhou are merely those who have missed its meaning. How could the Rites of Zhou itself deserve criticism?

Nevertheless, antiquity and the present concern the times; institutional arrangements concern methods; adaptation concerns the people who undertake it. Times do not remain the same, and methods accordingly differ. Thus later ages have often followed the outlines of Zhou's establishment of offices, but to apply its summonses to assemblies and its orders for requisitions today would cause harassment. Hence the saying: “To transform and shape things depends upon change; to comprehend them with spirit-like insight depends upon the person.”

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
第四問
王應時
同考試官敎諭謝批聖人敬天理地之意存乎術數
之外子能言之可謂知聖人矣
考試官學正李批推原天地之理切於民用有見
考試官敎授向批談術而本之理是善言天地者
用天之道者善知天者也因地之利者善
知地者也夫天垂象而聖人觀之以立占
作曆授時取於此焉故曰用天之道也地
===
列形而聖人察之以宜民體國經野行其
制焉故曰因地之利也觀天察地凡以為
民則聖人之知天非妄也民功興而天道
昭矣聖人之知地非迂也民物阜而地利
永矣故曰聖人善知天地也執事發策下
詢承學以天地之理愚也學無師授性乏
通悟何足以知之然亦甞有聞於載籍矣
請掇拾以對夫乾象之說何昉乎自黃帝
命羲和占日月車區占星氣於是有星官
punctuated:
第四問
王應時
同考試官敎諭謝批：聖人敬天理地之意，存乎術數之外。子能言之，可謂知聖人矣。
考試官學正李批：推原天地之理，切於民用，有見。
考試官敎授向批：談術而本之理，是善言天地者。
用天之道者，善知天者也；因地之利者，善知地者也。夫天垂象，而聖人觀之以立占，作曆授時，取於此焉，故曰用天之道也。地列形，而聖人察之以宜民，體國經野，行其制焉，故曰因地之利也。觀天察地，凡以為民，則聖人之知天非妄也，民功興而天道昭矣；聖人之知地非迂也，民物阜而地利永矣。故曰聖人善知天地也。執事發策，下詢承學以天地之理。愚也學無師授，性乏通悟，何足以知之？然亦甞有聞於載籍矣，請掇拾以對。夫乾象之說何昉乎？自黃帝命羲和占日月，車區占星氣，於是有星官
translation_en:
Fourth Policy Question
Wang Yingshi
Associate Examiner Xie, Instructor, comments: “The sages’ intent in revering Heaven and ordering Earth lies beyond technical and numerical arts. You can articulate this and may thus be said to understand the sages.”
Examiner Li, School Director, comments: “Traces the principles of Heaven and Earth to their sources and relates them closely to practical use for the people. Insightful.”
Examiner Xiang, Professor, comments: “Discusses techniques while grounding them in principle: this is someone who speaks well of Heaven and Earth.”
Those who employ the Way of Heaven understand Heaven well; those who make use of Earth’s advantages understand Earth well. Heaven displays its signs, and the sages observe them to establish prognostications. They draw upon these to make calendars and announce the seasons. Hence this is called employing the Way of Heaven. Earth presents its forms, and the sages examine them to provide suitable conditions for the people. They lay out the capital and demarcate the countryside, putting their institutions into practice. Hence this is called making use of Earth’s advantages. Observing Heaven and examining Earth are alike undertaken for the people. Thus the sages’ understanding of Heaven is no idle fancy: the people’s undertakings flourish, and the Way of Heaven becomes manifest. The sages’ understanding of Earth is no impractical pursuit: the people and all things prosper, and Earth’s benefits endure. Hence it is said that the sages understand Heaven and Earth well.
You, honored examiners, have issued a policy question, condescending to ask us students about the principles of Heaven and Earth. I, unworthy as I am, have studied without instruction from a teacher and lack an innate capacity for comprehensive understanding. How could I adequately understand them? Yet I have encountered something of them in written works. Allow me to gather these scattered accounts and reply.
Where did explanations of celestial phenomena originate? The Yellow Emperor commanded Xi and He to divine by the sun and moon, and Chequ [?] to divine by the stars and celestial emanations. Thereupon there were celestial officials …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
之書而高陽氏則以南正重司天始有專
官矣至唐虞星鳥星火之分識璿璣玉衡
之首察以求七政之齊而周官則以馮相
保章氏世其業矣其後言天體者有宣夜
周髀渾天宣夜有名而無術周髀有術而
無驗惟渾天之法揚子雲謂其近理以其
能祖述璣衡而後世六合三辰四遊之儀
皆其制之傳也善星官者有巫咸甘德石
申巫咸之書無所考見而甘石善於推歩
===
獨爲星經之祖凡今三垣五宮兩極十二
辰野五星列宿干支方位之說皆其術之
餘也楚魏而下代有其人如漢之洛下閎
鮮于妄人唐之李淳風僧一行皆以其術
著名當時而一行之穎悟絕人象數精博
其最優歟宋之沈括邵堯夫元之許平仲
郭守敬各以其說發明天道而守敬之立
法精詳度越千古其尤善歟要之聖人首
出庶物先天不違故能敬天觀象治曆明
punctuated: 之書，而高陽氏則以南正重司天，始有專官矣。至唐虞，星鳥星火之分識，璿璣玉衡之首察，以求七政之齊；而周官則以馮相、保章氏世其業矣。其後言天體者，有宣夜、周髀、渾天。宣夜有名而無術，周髀有術而無驗；惟渾天之法，揚子雲謂其近理，以其能祖述璣衡，而後世六合、三辰、四遊之儀，皆其制之傳也。善星官者，有巫咸、甘德、石申。巫咸之書無所考見，而甘石善於推歩，獨爲星經之祖。凡今三垣、五宮、兩極、十二辰野、五星、列宿、干支、方位之說，皆其術之餘也。楚魏而下，代有其人，如漢之洛下閎、鮮于妄人，唐之李淳風、僧一行，皆以其術著名當時。而一行之穎悟絕人，象數精博，其最優歟？宋之沈括、邵堯夫，元之許平仲、郭守敬，各以其說發明天道。而守敬之立法精詳，度越千古，其尤善歟？要之，聖人首出庶物，先天不違，故能敬天觀象，治曆明
translation_en:
…writings on the stars; under Gaoyang, Chong, the Director of the South, was charged with celestial affairs, and a dedicated office first came into being. In the time of Tang and Yu, the Bird and Fire asterisms were separately identified, and the rotating mechanism and jade sighting tube were examined as a primary task, to bring the seven celestial regulators—the sun, moon, and five planets—into proper order. Under the offices of Zhou, the Astronomer and Astrologer transmitted this work hereditarily.

Later explanations of the structure of the heavens included the Xuanye, Zhoubi, and Huntian theories. Xuanye possessed a name but no method; Zhoubi possessed a method but lacked verification. Only the Huntian method was considered close to the underlying principles by Yang Ziyun, because it could carry forward the tradition of the rotating mechanism and sighting tube. The later Instruments of the Six Directions, Three Celestial Bodies, and Four Movements all perpetuated its design.

Those skilled in stellar astronomy included Wu Xian, Gan De, and Shi Shen. Wu Xian’s writings can no longer be consulted or examined, but Gan and Shi excelled in astronomical calculation and stood alone as the founders of the stellar canon. Present-day explanations of the Three Enclosures, Five Palaces, two poles, twelve celestial divisions and their corresponding terrestrial regions, five planets, constellations, heavenly stems and earthly branches, and directional positions are all legacies of their methods.

From the times of Chu and Wei onward, every age produced such men. Luoxia Hong and Xianyu Wangren of the Han, and Li Chunfeng and the monk Yixing of the Tang, all gained renown in their day for these arts. Yet Yixing’s keen understanding surpassed others, and his knowledge of celestial configurations and numerical relations was both precise and extensive. Was he perhaps the finest of them? Shen Kuo and Shao Yaofu of the Song, and Xu Pingzhong and Guo Shoujing of the Yuan, each illuminated the workings of Heaven through their explanations. Shoujing’s establishment of methods was precise and detailed, surpassing all preceding ages. Was he perhaps especially accomplished?

In essence, the sage rises above the myriad beings and, even when acting before Heaven, does not depart from it. Thus he can revere Heaven, observe celestial phenomena, regulate the calendar, and make clear…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
時以命其臣而後世則沿襲古制隨時脩
改間有作者又多業非師授言以人殊卒
莫有辨而正之者然則知天之道不亦難
哉夫堪輿之說何始乎維昔黃帝畫野分
州得國萬區當時必有所主之人顓頊氏
命北正黎司地以主民亦必有所治之職
而皆無所於見堪輿亦古掌地之官名嘗
觀呂才著卜宅篇引堪輿經載黃帝對天
老言五姓之說則其書尚存於唐而今則
===
無傳矣周禮惟王建國辨方正位而土方
氏有掌土圭之法大司空有土宜之法皆
以土地相民宅而建邦邑他日周公洛邑
之卜衛文方中之定率用是道而聖人所
以為民之意從可識矣蓋廣谷大川異制
民生其間異俗要亦地氣使然而其風雨
所會陰陽所和者則百物阜安故司馬遷
作地志歷敘天下民俗物產各因其地而
周人辨之必詳者其固用地宜以阜民者
punctuated:
時，以命其臣。而後世則沿襲古制，隨時脩改，間有作者，又多業非師授，言以人殊，卒莫有辨而正之者。然則知天之道，不亦難哉？
夫堪輿之說何始乎？維昔黃帝畫野分州，得國萬區，當時必有所主之人。顓頊氏命北正黎司地以主民，亦必有所治之職，而皆無所於見。堪輿亦古掌地之官名。嘗觀呂才著《卜宅篇》，引《堪輿經》，載黃帝對天老言五姓之說，則其書尚存於唐，而今則無傳矣。《周禮》：「惟王建國，辨方正位。」而土方氏有掌土圭之法，大司空有土宜之法，皆以土地相民宅而建邦邑。他日周公洛邑之卜、衛文方中之定，率用是道，而聖人所以為民之意從可識矣。蓋廣谷大川異制，民生其間異俗，要亦地氣使然。而其風雨所會、陰陽所和者，則百物阜安。故司馬遷作地志，歷敘天下民俗物產，各因其地。而周人辨之必詳者，其固用地宜以阜民者
translation_en:
…the seasons, and charge their ministers accordingly. Later generations, however, followed ancient institutions, revising them as circumstances required. From time to time innovators appeared, but their learning was often not transmitted by teachers, and their accounts differed from person to person. In the end, no one distinguished and corrected these discrepancies. Is it not difficult, then, to understand the Way of Heaven?
Where did the teachings of geomancy (kanyu) originate? Long ago, the Yellow Emperor marked out the land and divided it into regions, obtaining ten thousand domains. At that time there must have been people responsible for them. Zhuanxu commanded Li, the Northern Director, to administer the earth and oversee the people; he too must have held an office with defined responsibilities. Yet no evidence of either remains to be seen. Kanyu was also the name of an ancient office responsible for the earth. I once read Lü Cai’s Essay on Divining Dwelling Sites, which quotes the Classic of Geomancy and records the Yellow Emperor speaking to Tianlao about the theory of the five surnames. That book therefore still existed in the Tang, but it is no longer transmitted today. The Rites of Zhou states: “When the king establishes a capital, he distinguishes the directions and determines the proper positions.” The Director of Land Measurement had methods for using the earth gnomon, and the Minister of Works had methods for determining the suitability of soils. Both assessed sites for the people’s dwellings according to the land and established states and settlements. Later, the Duke of Zhou’s divination concerning Luoyi and Duke Wen of Wei’s determination of his site when the Ding constellation stood at the meridian followed this same Way. From this we can understand the sages’ intentions in acting for the people. Broad valleys and great rivers differ in their configurations, and the people living among them differ in their customs: ultimately, these differences are also brought about by the vital influences of the earth. Where winds and rains converge and yin and yang harmonize, all things flourish in security. Thus, when Sima Qian composed a geographical treatise [?], he successively described the customs and products of all under Heaven, each as conditioned by its locality. As for the people of Zhou, who invariably distinguished these matters in detail, surely they were making use of the land’s suitability to bring prosperity to the people …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
歟王公設險以守其國故古稱關中天府
之國百二之勝婁敬進說於漢高范仲淹
建議於宋帝智謀之士所見畧同至朱子
則又極言冀州風水之美豈非以其得地
勝而可以建國者歟若分野之說則又以
天星地域合而言之也其說本於天官星
土之辨不爲無據然觀史傳所載如梓慎
知宋鄭之饑史墨知越之有吳往往徵驗
似未可以星野之不相值而盡疑之也要
===
之聖人德業博厚配地無疆故能相理地
宜體國經野以奠其民而後世則承藉餘
休輯寧幹止間有說者又多流於小數泥
於致遠卒無有明而用之者然則知地之
道不亦難哉善乎唐一行之議曰原古人
所以重曆數之意將以恭授人時欽若乾
象而不在於渾蓋之是非其所以步圭景
之意將以節宣和氣輔相物宜而不在於
辰次之周徑君子謂其言之合理方今
punctuated:
歟？王公設險以守其國，故古稱關中天府之國，百二之勝。婁敬進說於漢高，范仲淹建議於宋帝，智謀之士所見畧同。至朱子，則又極言冀州風水之美，豈非以其得地勝而可以建國者歟？若分野之說，則又以天星地域合而言之也。其說本於天官星土之辨，不爲無據。然觀史傳所載，如梓慎知宋鄭之饑，史墨知越之有吳，往往徵驗，似未可以星野之不相值而盡疑之也。
要之，聖人德業博厚，配地無疆，故能相理地宜，體國經野，以奠其民。而後世則承藉餘休，輯寧幹止，間有說者，又多流於小數，泥於致遠，卒無有明而用之者。然則知地之道，不亦難哉？善乎唐一行之議曰：「原古人所以重曆數之意，將以恭授人時，欽若乾象，而不在於渾蓋之是非；其所以步圭景之意，將以節宣和氣，輔相物宜，而不在於辰次之周徑。」君子謂其言之合理。方今
translation_en:
…was this not so? Kings and dukes establish defensive barriers to protect their states. Thus, since antiquity, Guanzhong has been called a land of heavenly abundance, possessing the strategic advantage whereby two men could withstand a hundred. Lou Jing presented his counsel to Emperor Gao of Han, and Fan Zhongyan submitted his proposals to the Song emperor: these men of wisdom and resourcefulness held broadly similar views. Zhu Xi, moreover, spoke most emphatically of the excellence of Jizhou’s winds and waters. Was this not because its geographical advantages made it suitable for establishing a capital?
As for the theory of celestial correspondences with terrestrial regions, it discusses the stars in heaven and regions on earth together. This theory derives from the celestial officials’ distinctions between stars and their associated territories, and is therefore not without foundation. Yet consider what is recorded in the histories: Zi Shen foresaw famine in Song and Zheng, and Shi Mo foresaw Yue’s possession of Wu. Such predictions were repeatedly borne out. It would seem that we cannot doubt them all merely because the stars and their corresponding terrestrial regions do not align.
In sum, the sages’ virtue and achievements were broad and substantial, matching the earth in their boundlessness. Thus they could examine and order the land according to its suitability, lay out capitals and demarcate the countryside, and thereby settle their people securely. Later generations relied on the blessings they inherited, maintaining peace and stability [?]. Those who occasionally advanced explanations mostly strayed into petty techniques and became hampered in extending their understanding to broader matters [?]; ultimately, none understood these principles clearly and put them to use. Is not the way of understanding the earth difficult indeed?
Excellent was the argument of Yi Xing of the Tang, who said: “If we investigate why the ancients valued calendrical calculation, their intention was respectfully to communicate the seasons to the people and reverently to follow the patterns of heaven; it did not lie in deciding between the merits of the celestial-sphere and canopy theories. Their intention in measuring the gnomon’s shadow was to regulate and disseminate harmonious vital forces and assist all things in attaining their proper conditions; it did not lie in the circumferences and diameters of the celestial stations.” The gentleman considers these words consonant with reason. At present …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
聖人御極天位乎上而三辰順序地位乎下而
民物咸若蓋以致中和之功而運之於治
化兼歷代之制而守之於臣工億萬世無
疆之休端在是矣執事以爲何如
第五問
洪世遷
考試官學正李批通變宜民深得行法之意正作
以此鋪叙可占其用世之志矣
考試官敎授向批有斷有處錄之
===
興天下之利者在於宜民行天下之法者
在於通變變不通則無以善法民不宜則
無以善政所謂通變者酌時勢而損益之
非以紊夫法也所謂宜民者即土俗而權
度之非以徇夫人也通變宜民則政善民
安以之行法則不泥以之興利則可久又
何患於事不成而民不信哉執事下策承
學以錢幣通塞爲問是蓋有意於經國裕
民利用厚生之道愚也何足以知之然亦
punctuated:
聖人御極，天位乎上而三辰順序，地位乎下而民物咸若。蓋以致中和之功而運之於治化，兼歷代之制而守之於臣工，億萬世無疆之休，端在是矣。執事以爲何如？

第五問
洪世遷
考試官學正李批：通變宜民，深得行法之意。正作以此鋪叙，可占其用世之志矣。
考試官敎授向批：有斷有處，錄之。

興天下之利者在於宜民，行天下之法者在於通變。變不通則無以善法，民不宜則無以善政。所謂通變者，酌時勢而損益之，非以紊夫法也；所謂宜民者，即土俗而權度之，非以徇夫人也。通變宜民，則政善民安；以之行法則不泥，以之興利則可久，又何患於事不成而民不信哉？執事下策承學，以錢幣通塞爲問，是蓋有意於經國裕民、利用厚生之道。愚也何足以知之？然亦
translation_en:
…The sage sovereign occupies the throne; Heaven holds its place above, and the three celestial luminaries follow their proper sequence; Earth holds its place below, and the people and all things flourish in due order. Through the achievement of equilibrium and harmony, these principles are put into practice in government and moral transformation; the institutions of successive dynasties are brought together and upheld by the officials. Here indeed lies the foundation of boundless blessings for countless generations. What is your judgment on this?

Fifth Question
Hong Shiqian
Examiner Li, School Instructor, comments: “Adapting to change and meeting the people's needs: this shows a deep understanding of the purpose of implementing laws. The main essay develops its exposition on this basis, allowing us to discern his aspiration to serve the world.”
Examiner Xiang, Prefectural School Professor, comments: “He shows judgment and offers solutions. Accept him.”

Promoting benefits throughout the realm depends on meeting the people's needs; implementing laws throughout the realm depends on adapting to change. Without adaptation to change, laws cannot be made sound; without meeting the people's needs, government cannot be made good. What is called adapting to change means weighing the circumstances of the times and making additions or reductions accordingly; it does not mean throwing the laws into disorder. What is called meeting the people's needs means weighing measures in light of local customs; it does not mean yielding to people's wishes. When change is accommodated and the people's needs are met, government is good and the people are at peace. Applying this approach to laws avoids rigidity; applying it to the promotion of benefits makes them enduring. Why, then, fear that undertakings will fail or that the people will lack trust?

You have presented a policy question to us students, asking about the circulation and obstruction of coinage. This surely reflects your concern with the way to order the state, enrich the people, make resources useful, and improve livelihoods. How could someone as ignorant as I be fit to understand this? Yet I too…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
竊有見焉夫國之有財賦猶人之有元氣
也養身者當益其氣經國者當裕其財錢
也者所以制財貨之源權百物之本也布
帛不可以尺寸爲交菽粟不可以杪勺相
貿錢之爲質操之易持積之不弊以通有
無以定貴賤是其爲物雖小而其爲用甚
大司馬芝曰用錢非徒豐國亦所以省刑
是錢幣之行不可以不講也粤稽之古太
公立九府圜法曰泉者流通如泉也曰布
===
者宣布如布也命名之義蓋有取於此矣
而鄭樵乃謂泉言其形布言其用者吾敢
據以爲然哉管子謂湯鑄莊山之金以贖
人之鬻禹鑄歷山之金以救人之困鑄金
之意蓋因歲儉而爲之也而周禮之司市
所謂凶荒則市無征而作布豈亦禹湯之
遺意歟自是而行於漢高帝作莢錢所以
懲秦之重也其後易而爲八銖爲四銖爲
五銖法因時變名亦多矣而輕重適均者
punctuated:
竊有見焉。夫國之有財賦，猶人之有元氣也。養身者當益其氣，經國者當裕其財。錢也者，所以制財貨之源、權百物之本也。布帛不可以尺寸爲交，菽粟不可以杪勺相貿。錢之爲質，操之易持，積之不弊，以通有無，以定貴賤。是其爲物雖小，而其爲用甚大。司馬芝曰：「用錢非徒豐國，亦所以省刑。」是錢幣之行，不可以不講也。
粤稽之古，太公立九府圜法。曰泉者，流通如泉也；曰布者，宣布如布也。命名之義，蓋有取於此矣。而鄭樵乃謂泉言其形、布言其用者，吾敢據以爲然哉？管子謂湯鑄莊山之金以贖人之鬻，禹鑄歷山之金以救人之困。鑄金之意，蓋因歲儉而爲之也。而《周禮》之司市所謂「凶荒則市無征而作布」，豈亦禹湯之遺意歟？自是而行於漢，高帝作莢錢，所以懲秦之重也。其後易而爲八銖，爲四銖，爲五銖，法因時變，名亦多矣。而輕重適均者
translation_en:
…I venture to offer an observation. A state’s revenues are like a person’s vital energy. Those who nourish the body should replenish its energy; those who administer the state should augment its wealth. Coin is the means of regulating the sources of wealth and goods, and the basis for determining the relative value of all commodities. Cloth and silk cannot be exchanged by the foot or inch, nor beans and grain traded in tiny spoonfuls [?]. As material objects, coins are easy to carry in the hand and do not deteriorate when stored. They enable exchange between those who have goods and those who lack them, and establish relative prices. Thus, although small in themselves, their usefulness is very great. Sima Zhi said: “Using coin not only enriches the state; it also reduces punishments.” The circulation of currency therefore requires careful consideration.
Looking back into antiquity, the Grand Duke established the currency system of the Nine Treasuries. Currency was called quan, “spring,” because it circulated like spring water; it was called bu, “cloth,” because it spread abroad like cloth. These names presumably drew their meaning from this. Yet Zheng Qiao asserted that quan referred to its shape and bu to its use. Dare I accept his assertion as correct? The Guanzi says that Tang cast metal from Mount Zhuang to redeem people who had been sold, and Yu cast metal from Mount Li to relieve people in distress. Their intention in casting metal currency was evidently to respond to years of scarcity. And when the Director of Markets section of the Rites of Zhou speaks of “levying no market taxes during famine and issuing currency,” might this likewise preserve the intention of Yu and Tang? The practice continued into the Han, when Emperor Gao made pod coins to remedy the excessive weight of Qin coinage. Subsequently these were replaced by eight-zhu, four-zhu, and five-zhu coins. The regulations changed with the times, and the names were numerous. But as for those whose weight struck just the right balance…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
惟五銖乎自是而行於唐則開通鑄於武
德所以易隋之舊也其後變而為開元為
天寶為乾元名以世易制亦善矣而經久
可行者惟開元乎呂祖謙曰論太重則有
所謂直百當十論太輕則有所謂榆莢三
銖然而皆不得中惟五銖開元銖兩之多
寡鼓鑄之精密相望而不可易蓋有見于
此也宋元以來更造不一或費多而利不
歸上或令煩而事不便民更革無常未容
===
悉議惟我
國家因時定制設局鼓鑄酌輕重之宜行斂
散之法相兼前代布之民間泉貨流通遐
邇歸會百有餘年上無紛更之擾下無匱
乏之患顧行之旣久民自殊風大江以北
三幣並行大江以南錢不為市此豈錢之
不行哉公府不入則富者積而無施勢窒
不藏則貧民得之無用是宜其滯也執事
之言曰南北異俗不可强同豈獨南北然
punctuated:
惟五銖乎？自是而行於唐，則開通鑄於武德，所以易隋之舊也。其後變而為開元、為天寶、為乾元，名以世易，制亦善矣，而經久可行者惟開元乎？呂祖謙曰：「論太重，則有所謂直百、當十；論太輕，則有所謂榆莢、三銖。然而皆不得中，惟五銖、開元，銖兩之多寡、鼓鑄之精密，相望而不可易。」蓋有見于此也。宋元以來，更造不一，或費多而利不歸上，或令煩而事不便民，更革無常，未容悉議。
惟我國家因時定制，設局鼓鑄，酌輕重之宜，行斂散之法，相兼前代，布之民間，泉貨流通，遐邇歸會。百有餘年，上無紛更之擾，下無匱乏之患。顧行之旣久，民自殊風：大江以北，三幣並行；大江以南，錢不為市。此豈錢之不行哉？公府不入，則富者積而無施；勢窒不藏，則貧民得之無用，是宜其滯也。執事之言曰：「南北異俗，不可强同。」豈獨南北然
translation_en:
…was it only the five-zhu coin? Thereafter, under the Tang, Kaitong coins [?] were cast during the Wude reign to replace the old Sui currency. Subsequently these changed to Kaiyuan, Tianbao, and Qianyuan coins. Their names changed with the times, and their standards were also sound; yet was it only the Kaiyuan coin that remained usable over the long term? Lü Zuqian said: “As for excessively heavy denominations, there were the so-called ‘worth a hundred’ and ‘equivalent to ten’ coins; as for excessively light ones, there were the ‘elm-seed’ and three-zhu coins. None, however, attained the proper balance. Only the five-zhu and Kaiyuan coins matched one another in their weight and the precision of their casting, and could not be superseded.” He evidently understood this point. Since the Song and Yuan, successive issues have varied: sometimes costs were great but the profit did not accrue to the government; sometimes regulations were burdensome and their implementation inconvenient for the people. Changes were incessant, and there is no room to discuss them all.
Our dynasty alone established standards suited to the times, set up minting offices, determined suitable weights, and put into practice methods of collecting and disbursing coin. It circulated its coins among the people alongside those of preceding dynasties. Currency flowed freely, converging from near and far. For more than a hundred years, those above suffered no disruption from repeated changes, and those below had no anxiety over shortages. Yet after such long use, local practices have diverged: north of the Great River, three currencies circulate together; south of it, coins are not used in market transactions. Is this really an inherent inability of coins to circulate? If government offices do not accept them, the rich accumulate them but have nowhere to spend them; if powerful households [?] do not keep them, poor people who acquire them have no use for them. It is natural, then, that their circulation should stagnate. You gentlemen say: “The north and south have different customs and cannot be forced into uniformity.” But is this true only of the north and south…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
哉夫土貨旣殊貿鬻自異利於都邑之肆
者不入徐揚之市便於荆郢之邦者礙乎
兗洛之域王澄嘗言之矣自今觀之有行
於一郡而滯於一邑有行於一邑而滯於
一鄉者愚以為此豈民風之殊要在轉移
之耳執事又謂嶺海之間以之貿遷若有
感於閩廣通塞之異而求所以錢幣大行
民情俱協之道愚以為廣谷大川異制民
生其間異俗君子脩其敎不易其俗齊其
===
政不易其宜斯王制之所以經綸天下也
何則民俗旣久更化難施積習已深作新
易擾苟非通變豈能樂成考之周禮外府
掌邦布之入出共其財用之幣齎賜予之
財凡邦之小用皆受焉泉府掌邦市之征
布斂市之不售貨之滯於民者夫周禮掌
財之官非一職也而泉布獨於二府隷焉
者何邪蓋載齎之出入非錢不能以致遠
因其小用者而受之耳貿易之出入非錢
punctuated: 哉？夫土貨旣殊，貿鬻自異。利於都邑之肆者，不入徐揚之市；便於荆郢之邦者，礙乎兗洛之域。王澄嘗言之矣。自今觀之，有行於一郡而滯於一邑，有行於一邑而滯於一鄉者。愚以為此豈民風之殊？要在轉移之耳。執事又謂嶺海之間以之貿遷，若有感於閩廣通塞之異，而求所以錢幣大行、民情俱協之道。愚以為廣谷大川異制，民生其間異俗，君子脩其敎，不易其俗；齊其政，不易其宜。斯《王制》之所以經綸天下也。何則？民俗旣久，更化難施；積習已深，作新易擾。苟非通變，豈能樂成？考之《周禮》，外府掌邦布之入出，共其財用之幣、齎賜予之財，凡邦之小用皆受焉。泉府掌邦市之征布，斂市之不售、貨之滯於民者。夫《周禮》掌財之官非一職也，而泉布獨於二府隷焉者，何邪？蓋載齎之出入，非錢不能以致遠，因其小用者而受之耳。貿易之出入，非錢
translation_en:
…is this so? Local products differ, and trade naturally differs accordingly. What is advantageous in the shops of the capital does not enter the markets of Xu and Yang; what is convenient in the lands of Jing and Ying encounters obstacles in the regions of Yan and Luo. Wang Cheng once spoke of this. Looking at the present, there are coins that circulate within one prefecture but stagnate in a particular county, and coins that circulate within one county but stagnate in a particular township. In my humble view, can this really be due to differences in popular customs? The essential thing is simply to redirect their circulation. You further say that coins are used for trade in the region of the Ling mountains and the sea. It seems that, struck by the differences between Min and Guang in the ease or obstruction of circulation, you seek a way for coinage to circulate widely while accommodating the inclinations of all the people.

In my humble view, broad valleys and great rivers differ in their configuration, and the people living among them differ in their customs. The gentleman cultivates their instruction without changing their customs, and brings order to their government without changing what suits their circumstances. This is how the “Royal Regulations” provides for ordering the world. Why is this? Once popular customs are long established, reform is difficult to carry out; once accumulated habits are deeply rooted, renewal readily causes disturbance. Without adapting to changing circumstances, how could the people take pleasure in the result?

Examining the Rites of Zhou, we find that the Outer Treasury manages the receipt and disbursement of the state's money, supplying the currency for its expenditures and the funds for grants and gifts; all the state's minor expenditures draw upon it. The Coin Treasury manages the money collected as levies in the state's markets and purchases goods that remain unsold in the markets or lie idle in the people's hands. In the Rites of Zhou, responsibility for managing wealth belongs to more than one office. Why, then, is coinage assigned exclusively to these two treasuries? Because, in transporting funds in and out, only money can reach distant places; it is therefore received for minor expenditures. In the inflow and outflow of trade, without money…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
不得以兼濟因民之貨售者而通之耳是
蓋上下相承循環無端今欲行之亦曰流
通之機在上而不在下轉移之術以公而
不以私宋儒有曰古者制賦以穀制祿以
田則錢之權輕是以不行今制賦之法已
定如漕兌之正額無容議矣其他如郡邑
之存留以之而兼輸得無不可乎制祿之
法已定如
上供之正數無容議矣其他如百官羣吏之俸
===
給以之而兼支得無不可乎收之於課稅
者則發之於工役入之於罪贖者則出之
於賑貸里甲之雜辦以之其酬應不可用
乎徭役之差科以之其傭募不可散乎是
其輸者乃所以爲支其出者即所以爲入
其在官者即其在民其在私者即其在公
者也公私交利上下兼濟何必驅之以刑
脅之以威而後爲可行哉然則變通之道
孰有踰於此乎雖然濬流者當導其源齊
punctuated: 不得以兼濟，因民之貨售者而通之耳。是蓋上下相承，循環無端。今欲行之，亦曰：流通之機在上而不在下，轉移之術以公而不以私。宋儒有曰：「古者制賦以穀，制祿以田，則錢之權輕，是以不行。」今制賦之法已定，如漕兌之正額，無容議矣。其他如郡邑之存留，以之而兼輸，得無不可乎？制祿之法已定，如上供之正數，無容議矣。其他如百官羣吏之俸給，以之而兼支，得無不可乎？收之於課稅者，則發之於工役；入之於罪贖者，則出之於賑貸。里甲之雜辦，以之，其酬應不可用乎？徭役之差科，以之，其傭募不可散乎？是其輸者乃所以爲支，其出者即所以爲入，其在官者即其在民，其在私者即其在公者也。公私交利，上下兼濟，何必驅之以刑、脅之以威，而後爲可行哉？然則變通之道，孰有踰於此乎？雖然，濬流者當導其源，齊
translation_en:
…cannot serve the needs of all without coin; coin merely facilitates the sale of the people’s goods. Thus those above and below sustain one another in an unending cycle. If we wish to put this into practice now, we need only say: the key to circulation lies with those above, not those below, and the means of redirecting it rests with public administration, not private individuals. A Confucian scholar of the Song said: “In antiquity, taxes were assessed in grain and emoluments provided through land; consequently, coin had little importance and therefore did not circulate.”

Today the system of taxation is already fixed. Such matters as the regular quotas of grain delivered for transport by canal admit of no discussion. But for other items, such as revenues retained by prefectures and counties, might it not be permissible to remit part in coin? The system of emoluments is already fixed. Such matters as the prescribed amounts supplied to the throne admit of no discussion. But for other items, such as the salaries of the various officials and clerks, might it not be permissible to pay part in coin? What is collected in taxes could be disbursed for public works; what comes in through payments to redeem criminal penalties could go out as relief loans. For miscellaneous supplies furnished under the lijia household-registration system, could coin not be used to meet the associated expenses? For assessed labor-service obligations, could it not be distributed to hire workers? Thus what is remitted provides the means for expenditure, and what is paid out provides the means for receipts. Coin held by the authorities is also coin available to the people; coin in private hands is also coin available for public use. Public and private interests would both benefit, and those above and below would alike have their needs met. Why must people first be driven by punishment and cowed by authority before this can be made practicable? What method of adapting to circumstances could surpass this?

Nevertheless, those who deepen a stream must open up its source; those who would bring into order…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
末者當揣其本苟行之既久則錢必貴錢
貴則物賤物賤則民傷是所以便民者乃
所以敝之也其將何以處之亦曰通其源
而已故欲法之久也又當議鼓鑄之法重
私造之刑嚴薄惡之戒申磨鎔之令則庶
乎其可矣是在司計者主之非愚之所敢
與也
punctuated: 末者當揣其本。苟行之既久，則錢必貴；錢貴則物賤，物賤則民傷。是所以便民者，乃所以敝之也。其將何以處之？亦曰通其源而已。故欲法之久也，又當議鼓鑄之法，重私造之刑，嚴薄惡之戒，申磨鎔之令，則庶乎其可矣。是在司計者主之，非愚之所敢與也。
translation_en: …the branches must be regulated by attending to their root. If this practice continues for a long time, coins will inevitably become dear. When coins become dear, goods become cheap; when goods become cheap, the people suffer. Thus, what was intended to benefit the people becomes a means of impoverishing them. How, then, should this be addressed? Simply by opening up the source of supply. Therefore, if this policy is to endure, we must also consider methods of minting, increase the penalties for unauthorized coinage, strictly enforce prohibitions against thin and inferior coins, and reiterate the regulations against filing down and melting coins. Only then might it prove workable. This is for those responsible for fiscal administration to direct; it is not something in which I, in my ignorance, dare to intervene.

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
福建鄉試錄後序
福建鄉試錄成夢雲竊自慶
幸獲與諸執事周旋其間而
得人以告成事乃颺言于末
簡曰夫尼丘毓聖嵩嶽生申
山川之生材不誣也始夢雲
之應聘而至也陟霞嶺涉龍
===
江道武夷之麓望溟渤之洋
奮薄風雲吞吐日月信東南
之巨麗而山海之奇觀也進
而試其文則布體攄華陳高
發隱博而不泛朴而不俚浩
放而有制馳騁於子史而不
詭於道乃作而歎曰美哉郁
punctuated:
福建鄉試錄後序

福建鄉試錄成，夢雲竊自慶幸，獲與諸執事周旋其間，而得人以告成事，乃颺言于末簡曰：夫尼丘毓聖，嵩嶽生申，山川之生材不誣也。始夢雲之應聘而至也，陟霞嶺，涉龍江，道武夷之麓，望溟渤之洋，奮薄風雲，吞吐日月，信東南之巨麗，而山海之奇觀也。進而試其文，則布體攄華，陳高發隱，博而不泛，朴而不俚，浩放而有制，馳騁於子史而不詭於道。乃作而歎曰：「美哉！郁
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Fujian Provincial Examination

The Record of the Fujian Provincial Examination is complete. I, Mengyun, privately count myself fortunate to have worked here alongside the officials responsible and to have brought the undertaking to completion by finding worthy men. I therefore proclaim these words on its final pages: Niqiu nurtured the Sage, and Mount Song brought forth Shen; the claim that mountains and rivers produce men of talent is no falsehood. When I first arrived in response to the invitation, I climbed Xialing, crossed Longjiang, passed along the foot of Wuyi, and gazed toward the vast ocean. Stirring winds and clouds, swallowing and disgorging sun and moon—this is truly the grandeur of the southeast, a wondrous spectacle of mountains and sea.

Then, examining their compositions, I found that they arranged their structures and displayed their literary brilliance, expounded lofty ideas and revealed hidden meanings. They were learned without being diffuse, plain without being vulgar, expansive yet controlled. They ranged freely through the philosophical masters and histories without departing from the Way. Thereupon I rose and exclaimed: “How splendid! How richly …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
郁乎文獻之邦先民之遺澤
在焉其文可徵也夫天地之
精淑峙爲山岳流爲江河散
爲川阜瀦爲海瀆雖派别支
分自爲形體而源委脉絡各
有會同海者山水之鍾而風
氣之聚也閩地負山阻海自
===
武夷雄峙建溪回合盤鬱丹
青迆邐而東會爲芝城之勝
厚儲秀發滲漉凝結蓄爲瑰
奇煥爲文物真精靈淑盡萃
於人而士又得其最秀最靈
以爲之望宜閩士之多材也
夫和氏之玉登爲珪璧琮璜
punctuated:
郁乎文獻之邦！先民之遺澤在焉，其文可徵也。夫天地之精淑，峙爲山岳，流爲江河，散爲川阜，瀦爲海瀆。雖派别支分，自爲形體，而源委脉絡，各有會同。海者，山水之鍾而風氣之聚也。閩地負山阻海，自武夷雄峙，建溪回合，盤鬱丹青，迆邐而東，會爲芝城之勝。厚儲秀發，滲漉凝結，蓄爲瑰奇，煥爲文物。真精靈淑，盡萃於人，而士又得其最秀最靈，以爲之望。宜閩士之多材也！

夫和氏之玉，登爲珪璧琮璜，
translation_en:
…a flourishing land of letters and learned worthies! The beneficent legacy of its forebears remains here, and its writings bear witness to it. The pure and excellent essence of Heaven and Earth rises as mountains, flows as rivers, spreads out as streams and hills, and pools as seas and waterways. Although these divide into branches, each assuming its own form, their courses from source to outlet and their connecting veins all have points of convergence. The sea is where mountains and waters concentrate their influences and where the winds and vital energies gather. The land of Min has mountains at its back and the sea as its barrier. From the towering Wuyi Mountains, the Jian Stream winds and converges; amid coiling masses of cinnabar and azure, the landscape stretches eastward, coming together in the scenic splendor of Zhicheng. Richly stored, this essence issues forth in beauty; it seeps through and condenses, accumulating into rare wonders and shining forth as cultural refinement. Its genuine essence, numinous power, and purity all converge in human beings. Scholars, moreover, receive its finest and most numinous qualities and thus become the eminent figures of the region. It is fitting indeed that the scholars of Min should possess so many talents!

Now, the jade of Mr. He is fashioned into the ritual objects gui tablets, bi disks, cong tubes, and huang arcs …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
其精神則伏于崑岡汗血之
駒必渥洼乃良焉物固有然
者矣人才之美不但珪璧之
重黼黻之能不但致遠之用
也其鍾英萃美降神通氣以
成能于天下而發舒其精祥
此理之常無足怪者是故三
===
蘇生而眉山草木爲之改觀
二程出而伊洛源流因之益
遠九峰靈鷲固嶺表之卷石
也地不登于禹貢名不列于
職方自朱子結社以來而雲
谷少微之間遂爲名勝至有
裹糧千里快於一登此豈徒
punctuated: 其精神則伏于崑岡，汗血之駒必渥洼乃良焉。物固有然者矣。人才之美，不但珪璧之重；黼黻之能，不但致遠之用也。其鍾英萃美，降神通氣，以成能于天下，而發舒其精祥，此理之常，無足怪者。是故三蘇生，而眉山草木爲之改觀；二程出，而伊洛源流因之益遠。九峰、靈鷲，固嶺表之卷石也。地不登于《禹貢》，名不列于《職方》。自朱子結社以來，而雲谷、少微之間遂爲名勝，至有裹糧千里，快於一登。此豈徒
translation_en: …their vital essence lies hidden in the Kunlun heights; blood-sweating steeds must come from Wowa to be truly fine. Such is indeed the nature of things. The excellence of human talent is more than the preciousness of ritual jade tablets and discs; its capacity to adorn the affairs of state is more than the usefulness of a horse that carries one far. The gathering of excellence and beauty, the descent of spiritual potency and the circulation of vital energies, which bring talent to fruition in the world and unfold its pure, auspicious qualities—these are the normal workings of principle, nothing to marvel at. Thus, when the three Su were born, even the vegetation of Meishan took on a new aspect; when the two Cheng emerged, the intellectual streams of the Yi and Luo extended still farther. Jiufeng and Lingjiu were, to be sure, merely small outcrops beyond the mountain ranges. Their lands were not recorded in the Tribute of Yu, nor their names listed in the Offices of the Regions. Yet after Master Zhu formed a fellowship there, the area between Yungu and Shaowei became a celebrated scenic destination. Some even packed provisions and travelled a thousand li for the delight of a single ascent. Could this have been merely…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
以其風物哉故有斐者興淇
澳之歌而景行者動仰止之
念古人寄興懷人必本地靈
良有以也不然則勝母之里
曾子爲之不入而朝歌之市
墨子爲之回車豈非人之無
良祗以爲地辱耶爾諸士固
===
鍾山海之秀而生者行且進
試澤宮致用有日矣所以發
攄素蘊而闡洩地靈二三往
哲具有真模不必遠學也若
乃窮而學之達則棄之趨逐
紛華以自貽玷缺則是取誚
於山靈而見譏於海若也豈
punctuated:
以其風物哉？故有斐者興淇澳之歌，而景行者動仰止之念。古人寄興懷人，必本地靈，良有以也。不然，則勝母之里，曾子爲之不入；而朝歌之市，墨子爲之回車。豈非人之無良，祗以爲地辱耶？
爾諸士固鍾山海之秀而生者，行且進試澤宮，致用有日矣。所以發攄素蘊而闡洩地靈，二三往哲具有真模，不必遠學也。若乃窮而學之，達則棄之，趨逐紛華，以自貽玷缺，則是取誚於山靈，而見譏於海若也。豈
translation_en:
…merely because of its scenery and natural features? Thus, cultivated gentlemen inspired the song of the bends of the Qi River, and lofty conduct stirs thoughts of looking upward in admiration. The ancients, when expressing their feelings and cherishing the memory of others, invariably grounded these sentiments in the spiritual potency of a place; there was good reason for this. Otherwise, why did Zengzi refuse to enter the village of Shengmu, whose name means “Surpassing One’s Mother,” and Mozi turn his carriage back from the town of Chaoge, whose name means “Morning Song”? Is it not that human failings bring only disgrace upon a place?
You scholars were born with the finest essences of the mountains and sea concentrated within you. Soon you will advance to be tested in the examination hall, and the day when you put your abilities to use will come. As for bringing forth your long-cultivated attainments and manifesting the spiritual potency of your native land, those few earlier worthies all provide true models: you need not seek distant examples to emulate. But if you study their teachings while obscure and abandon them once successful, chasing glittering worldly splendors and thereby bringing blemishes upon yourselves, you will invite reproach from the mountain spirits and ridicule from Hairuo, the god of the sea. Would this not…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
不惜哉夢雲不佞與諸士有
一日之雅故靦縷而終告之
河南汝寧府光州儒學學正
李夢雲謹序
punctuated:
不惜哉！夢雲不佞，與諸士有一日之雅，故靦縷而終告之。
河南汝寧府光州儒學學正李夢雲謹序。
translation_en:
…would that not be regrettable! I, Mengyun, though untalented, have enjoyed a brief acquaintance with you scholars, and therefore diffidently offer these final words at length [?].
This preface is respectfully written by Li Mengyun, Instructor of the Confucian School of Guangzhou Subprefecture, Runing Prefecture, Henan.

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
飭新規百度惟貞內外允秩
乃合試提學副使熊汲副使
張謙先後所取士三千有奇
得中式者九十人錄其名氏
與文以
獻洪邁謹序而言曰人才之盛豈
偶然哉則嘗稽諸古昔以驗
punctuated: 飭新規，百度惟貞，內外允秩。乃合試提學副使熊汲、副使張謙先後所取士三千有奇，得中式者九十人，錄其名氏與文以獻。洪邁謹序而言曰：「人才之盛，豈偶然哉？則嘗稽諸古昔以驗
translation_en: …put the new regulations in order, so that all administrative measures were correct and affairs both within and without were duly ordered. They then assembled for examination the more than three thousand scholars previously selected, in succession, by Xiong Ji, Education Intendant holding the rank of Surveillance Vice Commissioner, and Zhang Qian, Surveillance Vice Commissioner. Ninety passed. Their names and compositions were recorded for presentation to the throne. Hong Mai respectfully composed this preface, saying: “Could such an abundance of talent be merely accidental? I have examined the evidence of antiquity to verify…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
國家縣隔八郡遂稱名藩衣冠
之族半於里巷一時能自表
見功業文章項背相望豈非
風氣盤鬱有待而開而聲敎
之漸被使然哉我
皇上躬脩文治益張前烈詩書禮
樂之澤流布宇内屬採禮官
===
議以文尚頗僻士習有關
勅羣有司舉士諸不應經義而謬
錄者罪其舉主匪以飾聽凡
以崇文敎而敦古朴也一時
待徵之士罔不回慮惕心仰
承
休德今其文之可錄者率平實典
punctuated: 國家縣隔八郡，遂稱名藩。衣冠之族半於里巷，一時能自表見，功業文章項背相望，豈非風氣盤鬱，有待而開，而聲敎之漸被使然哉？我皇上躬脩文治，益張前烈，詩書禮樂之澤流布宇内。屬採禮官議，以文尚頗僻，士習有關，勅羣有司舉士，諸不應經義而謬錄者，罪其舉主。匪以飾聽，凡以崇文敎而敦古朴也。一時待徵之士，罔不回慮惕心，仰承休德。今其文之可錄者，率平實典
translation_en:
…the realm, with its eight prefectures spread far apart [?], thus came to be known as a distinguished province. Families of officials and scholars make up half its neighborhoods. Those able to distinguish themselves in their time have followed one another in close succession through their achievements and writings. Was this not because its accumulated cultural vitality awaited an opportunity to unfold, and because the gradual spread of imperial instruction brought this about?
Our Emperor personally cultivates civil government, further extending the glorious achievements of his predecessors. The beneficent influence of the Odes, Documents, rites, and music spreads throughout the realm. Recently he adopted a proposal from the officials responsible for ritual: since literary preferences had become biased and unorthodox, with consequences for the habits of scholars, he commanded the responsible officials selecting candidates that whenever they wrongly accepted writings inconsistent with the meaning of the Classics, those who recommended the candidates should be punished. This was no mere pronouncement intended to impress its hearers; its whole purpose was to honor literary instruction and foster the simplicity of antiquity. All the scholars then awaiting selection reconsidered their thinking and made their hearts vigilant, reverently receiving his gracious virtue. Now those of their writings worthy of inclusion are generally straightforward, substantial, and classically…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
雅出入於經史而折衷於孔
孟蔚乎治世之能言曾未移
時而聲敎所被迎風雅化不
但俄頃之助已也於乎盛矣
夫人才之成雖不係於地而
卜宅者必期於仁里豪傑之
興固無待於時而潛德者尤
===
快於利見今夫秋葯漸之而
臭素絲染之而黑千里之駒
不經服習之敎不可以致遠
故學齊言者不楚傳而獲夜
光者不晝售魯無君子則子
賤無所取以成德世有文王
則中林野人且爲公侯之腹
punctuated:
雅，出入於經史而折衷於孔孟，蔚乎治世之能言！曾未移時，而聲敎所被，迎風雅化，不但俄頃之助已也。於乎盛矣！
夫人才之成，雖不係於地，而卜宅者必期於仁里；豪傑之興，固無待於時，而潛德者尤快於利見。今夫秋葯，漸之而臭；素絲，染之而黑。千里之駒，不經服習之敎，不可以致遠。故學齊言者不楚傳，而獲夜光者不晝售。魯無君子，則子賤無所取以成德；世有文王，則中林野人且爲公侯之腹
translation_en:
…elegant, ranging through the classics and histories while taking Confucius and Mencius as their ultimate standard: a flourishing display of eloquence worthy of a well-governed age! Before long, wherever the influence of imperial instruction reached, people responded to it and were refined. Its benefits were by no means merely momentary. Ah, how splendid!
Although the cultivation of talent does not depend upon a particular place, those choosing where to dwell invariably seek a neighborhood of benevolence. Although the emergence of outstanding men need not await a particular age, those whose virtue remains hidden especially rejoice in an opportunity to appear before a great man. Consider autumn angelica: steeping imparts its fragrance; white silk becomes black when dyed. A colt capable of traveling a thousand li cannot reach distant places without training and practice. Thus one learning the speech of Qi does not take a man of Chu as his tutor, and one who obtains a night-shining pearl does not offer it for sale by daylight. Had Lu possessed no gentlemen, Zijian would have had no one from whom to learn and perfect his virtue; when King Wen is present in the world, even rustic men dwelling deep in the woods may become the lords’ trusted …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
心何者明盛之會難逢而漸
染之化易成也是故道悅周
孔陳良不免於北學人存伊
洛游楊必期於遠遊爾諸士
生君子之鄉遺範餘休往往
而在蓋不必遠慕而有餘師
矣而況親炙
===
聖德之光而沐浴菁莪之化
文敎日宣而盛美益振宜人才
之盛獨見於
今日也夫士之生不幸不得其
地得其地矣又患不遇其時
今
聖明在上固才智奮庸之日也則
punctuated: 心。何者？明盛之會難逢，而漸染之化易成也。是故道悅周孔，陳良不免於北學；人存伊洛，游楊必期於遠遊。爾諸士生君子之鄉，遺範餘休往往而在，蓋不必遠慕而有餘師矣。而況親炙聖德之光，而沐浴菁莪之化，文敎日宣，而盛美益振，宜人才之盛獨見於今日也。夫士之生，不幸不得其地；得其地矣，又患不遇其時。今聖明在上，固才智奮庸之日也，則
translation_en: …trusted confidants. Why is this? An enlightened and flourishing age is hard to encounter, yet transformation through gradual influence is readily accomplished. Thus, delighting in the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, Chen Liang could not forgo studying in the north; while worthy men lived in the Yi and Luo region, You Zuo and Yang Shi were resolved to journey far to study. You scholars were born in a land of exemplary men, where surviving models and enduring blessings are everywhere to be found. Surely you have ample teachers without needing to seek distant exemplars. Moreover, you are directly illuminated by the radiance of the sage emperor’s virtue and bathed in the nurturing influence celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood.” As civil instruction spreads daily and its splendid achievements grow ever more manifest, it is fitting that talent should flourish uniquely today. A scholar may have the misfortune to be born in an unsuitable place; even if he finds the right place, he still fears that he may not encounter the right time. Now an enlightened sage reigns above: this is indeed the day for men of talent and wisdom to exert themselves in service. Then …

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
所以增光先達而仰答
明時責將誰諉哉故緣飾詩書譁
眾市譽以曲趨巧售者先民
之敝德詭辭謬進幼學壯違
以徼取富貴者
清朝之棄才有一於此是墜前脩
之光而干
===
明主之典非所以自靖而圖報也
夫豈惟主司之憂抑亦二三
子者之羞是舉也提督南贛
軍務右副都御史顧遂綏靖
一方文事有賴左參議夏寶
僉事利賓戴鯨韓柱張合署
都指揮僉事李翱盧鎧防翊
punctuated:
所以增光先達而仰答明時，責將誰諉哉？故緣飾詩書、譁眾市譽，以曲趨巧售者，先民之敝德；詭辭謬進、幼學壯違，以徼取富貴者，清朝之棄才。有一於此，是墜前脩之光而干明主之典，非所以自靖而圖報也。夫豈惟主司之憂，抑亦二三子者之羞！
是舉也，提督南贛軍務右副都御史顧遂，綏靖一方，文事有賴。左參議夏寶，僉事利賓、戴鯨、韓柱、張合，署都指揮僉事李翱、盧鎧，防翊
translation_en:
…as for bringing added glory to their distinguished predecessors and repaying this enlightened age, to whom could they shift that responsibility? Those who embellish their words with the Book of Odes and Book of Documents, courting the crowd and buying acclaim, seeking advancement through devious compliance and cunning self-promotion, exemplify conduct condemned by the ancients. Those who advance improperly through deceitful words, abandoning in adulthood what they learned in youth in pursuit of wealth and rank, are talents rejected by this pure court. To commit either fault is to dim the glory of earlier worthies and transgress the statutes of an enlightened ruler; it is no way to discharge one’s duty conscientiously and seek to repay imperial favor. Indeed, this would be not only a concern for the presiding examiners, but also a disgrace to you gentlemen!
For this examination, Gu Sui, Right Vice Censor-in-Chief and Superintendent of Military Affairs in Nan-Gan, secured peace throughout the region, providing the support on which literary affairs depended. Xia Bao, Left Administration Assistant Commissioner; Li Bin, Dai Jing, Han Zhu, and Zhang He, Surveillance Assistant Commissioners; and Li Ao and Lu Kai, acting Assistant Regional Military Commissioners, provided defense and protection…

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
宣勞入
覲右參議柯喬僉事徐緯署都指
揮僉事路正始事協議刑部
署員外郎事主事盧璘奉使
玆土樂觀厥成法皆得書者
也直隸蘇州府儒學教授向
洪邁謹序
punctuated:
宣勞。入覲右參議柯喬、僉事徐緯、署都指揮僉事路正，始事協議；刑部署員外郎事主事盧璘，奉使玆土，樂觀厥成。法皆得書者也。
直隸蘇州府儒學教授向洪邁謹序。
translation_en:
… rendered meritorious service. Ke Qiao, Right Assistant Administration Commissioner; Xu Wei, Assistant Surveillance Commissioner; and Lu Zheng, Acting Assistant Regional Military Commissioner, who went to court for an imperial audience, consulted together at the outset of this undertaking. Lu Lin, a Bureau Secretary acting as Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice, came to this region on an official mission and was pleased to witness its successful completion. By established convention, all are entitled to be recorded here.
Respectfully composed as a preface by Xiang Hongmai, Professor of the Confucian School of Suzhou Prefecture in the directly administered metropolitan region.

Fujian Provincial Examination, the Twenty-fifth Year of Jiajing (1546)

Supervising Official
Zhao Yingxiang, Investigating Censor serving as Regional Inspector of Fujian, had the courtesy name Bozheng and was from Changsha Guard, Huguang. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the yiwei year.

Proctors

Xiang Hongmai, Instructor at the Confucian School of Suzhou Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Jinggao and was from Cixi County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the jiachen year.

Chen Shou, Instructor at the Confucian School of Xun County, Daming Prefecture, Zhili, had the courtesy name Shupei. He was registered in an officer household of Xi'an Rear Guard, Shaanxi, and was a native of Macheng County, Huguang. He was a tribute scholar of the jiawu year.

translation_en:
Xia Zuo, Instructor of the Confucian School of Chenliu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan. His courtesy name was Changqing; he was registered in Yuan’an County, Huguang, and was a native of Fengcheng County, Jiangxi. He was a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the gengzi year.

title: 嘉靖二十五年福建鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
子曰參乎吾道一以貫之曾子曰唯子出
門人問曰何謂也曾子曰夫子之道忠
恕而已矣
極高明而道中庸
以友天下之善士爲未足又尚論古之人
頌其詩讀其書不知其人可乎是以論
其世也是尚友也
===
易
忠信所以進德也修辭立其誠所以居業
也
恒久也剛上而柔下雷風相與巽而動剛
柔皆應恒
夫易聖人之所以極深而研幾也
兼三才而兩之故易六畫而成卦分陰分
陽迭用柔剛故易六位而成章
書
punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

子曰：「參乎！吾道一以貫之。」曾子曰：「唯。」子出，門人問曰：「何謂也？」曾子曰：「夫子之道，忠恕而已矣。」

極高明而道中庸。

以友天下之善士爲未足，又尚論古之人。頌其詩，讀其書，不知其人，可乎？是以論其世也。是尚友也。

易

忠信所以進德也，修辭立其誠所以居業也。

恒，久也。剛上而柔下，雷風相與，巽而動，剛柔皆應，恒。

夫易，聖人之所以極深而研幾也。

兼三才而兩之，故易六畫而成卦；分陰分陽，迭用柔剛，故易六位而成章。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: “Shen! My Way is threaded together by a single principle.” Zengzi replied: “Yes.” When the Master went out, the disciples asked: “What did he mean?” Zengzi said: “The Master’s Way consists simply of wholehearted commitment and consideration for others.”

Reach the utmost heights of illumination while following the path of the Mean.

Considering friendship with the good scholars of the world insufficient, one goes further back to discuss the people of antiquity. When chanting their poems and reading their writings, can one fail to know what sort of people they were? Thus one examines the age in which they lived. This is to reach back in friendship.

Book of Changes

Loyalty and trustworthiness are the means of advancing virtue; refining one’s words and establishing sincerity are the means of abiding in one’s work.

Heng means enduring. The firm is above and the yielding below; thunder and wind act together; there is gentleness and movement; the firm and yielding all respond to one another: this is constancy.

The Changes is that by which the sages plumb the depths and investigate the first subtle signs of things.

It embraces the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—and doubles them; thus in the Changes six lines form a hexagram. Yin and yang are distinguished, and yielding and firm lines alternate in use; thus the six positions of the Changes form an ordered pattern.
